title: Visitor Pattern
oneLiner: Adds new operations across a whole class hierarchy without modifying any of those classes — by having the operation visit each one.

hero.name: The Emissary
hero.catchphrase: I bring the operation to you — you don't carry it yourself.
hero.power: Adds an entirely new operation across a class hierarchy (pricing, exporting, validating) without editing a single one of those classes.
hero.weakness: The trade-off flips: adding a brand-new shape to the hierarchy now means updating every existing visitor — easy to add operations, hard to add types.
hero.origin: The Emissary appeared after a shape library needed a new `exportToSvg()` operation, and adding it meant touching Circle, Square, Triangle, and eleven other shape classes just to add one method each.

story.problem: Adding an `exportToSvg()` method means editing Circle, Square, Triangle, and eleven other shape classes — one method added per class, just for this one operation. The next operation means doing it all over again.
story.solution: The Emissary introduces a `ShapeVisitor` interface with one method per shape type. Each shape gets a single `accept(visitor)` method that calls back into the visitor. New operations become new visitor classes — no shape class changes.
story.result: Adding `exportToSvg()` now means writing one new `SvgExportVisitor` class. None of the fourteen shape classes are touched.

before: Every new operation means editing every shape class
Shape classes accumulate unrelated operation-specific methods
Operations and data are tightly tangled together
after: Every new operation is one new visitor class
Shape classes stay focused purely on their own data
Operations and data are cleanly separated

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A pull request touches fourteen different shape files, adding one exportToSvg() method to each.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Fourteen files changed, for ONE new feature. And we'll do this again for exportToPdf() next sprint.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Emissary appears holding a single letter addressed to every shape, ready to visit each one in turn.
panels.speaker: The Emissary
panels.dialogue: Stop carrying the operation into every shape class. Let ME visit each shape instead — the shapes barely have to change at all.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Each shape gets one accept(visitor) method. SvgExportVisitor implements visitCircle(), visitSquare(), visitTriangle().
panels.speaker: The Emissary
panels.dialogue: shape.accept(visitor) calls back to visitor.visitCircle(shape) automatically. The operation lives entirely inside me — the visitor — not inside the shape.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: exportToPdf ships as one new visitor class. Zero shape files are touched.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One new visitor class, zero changes to any shape. That's the entire PR now.

useWhen: You need to add new, unrelated operations (export, pricing, validation) across a stable class hierarchy repeatedly.
The class hierarchy itself rarely changes, but the operations performed on it change or grow often.
You want to keep operation-specific logic out of the domain classes entirely, for a cleaner separation of concerns.
avoidWhen: The class hierarchy changes frequently — every new class means updating every existing visitor, which gets expensive fast.
You only need one operation, once — Visitor's ceremony isn't worth it for a single use case.
The language doesn't support double dispatch cleanly, making the boilerplate heavier than the benefit.
commonMistakes: Applying Visitor to a hierarchy that changes often — every new subclass forces updates to every existing visitor, which is exactly backwards from what you want.
Forgetting to implement a new shape type's `accept()` method, silently breaking every visitor that should have handled it.
Overusing Visitor for a single operation that would've been simpler as one ordinary method on the base class.
Letting visitors reach into shape internals instead of working through the shape's public interface, tightly coupling them anyway.
explanation.realWorldExample: AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) traversal in compilers and linters — one Visitor per operation (type-checking, code generation, formatting) walking a stable tree of node types — is the textbook real-world use of Visitor.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Why not just add exportToSvg() directly to each shape class?

conversation.speaker: The Emissary
conversation.message: You could — until the fifth unrelated operation shows up and every shape class is bloated with export/price/validate methods that have nothing to do with being a shape. I keep operations OUT of the data classes entirely.

conversation.speaker: The Emissary
conversation.message: Add a new shape — say, Hexagon — and every existing visitor needs a new visitHexagon() method. I trade 'easy to add operations' for 'hard to add types'. Know which one your codebase changes more often.

codeBattle.scenario: Your compiler's AST has 20 stable node types (numbers, strings, function calls, ...) and needs type-checking, code generation, and pretty-printing — three operations, likely more to come, over a hierarchy that rarely changes.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Emissary lets each new operation (type-checking, codegen, printing) become its own visitor class, without touching any of the 20 stable node classes.

quiz.question: What trade-off does Visitor make?
options: Adding new operations becomes easy; adding new classes to the hierarchy becomes hard
Adding new classes becomes easy; adding new operations becomes hard
Both adding operations and adding classes become equally easy
Visitor removes the need for any class hierarchy at all
quiz.answer: Adding new operations becomes easy; adding new classes to the hierarchy becomes hard
quiz.explanation: This is Visitor's defining trade-off — it inverts the usual difficulty of extending a hierarchy versus extending its operations.

quiz.question: What method does each element in the hierarchy typically implement to support Visitor?
options: accept(visitor), which calls back into the visitor's type-specific method
visit(), which performs the operation directly
clone(), to create a copy for the visitor to inspect
toString(), to convert itself into a visitor
quiz.answer: accept(visitor), which calls back into the visitor's type-specific method
quiz.explanation: The `accept()` call is what routes execution to the correct `visitX()` method on the visitor — the double dispatch mechanism.

quiz.question: When is Visitor a poor fit?
options: When the class hierarchy changes frequently, since every new type requires updating every existing visitor
When you need to add many new operations to a stable hierarchy
When operations should be kept separate from the data classes
When you're building a compiler or linter
quiz.answer: When the class hierarchy changes frequently, since every new type requires updating every existing visitor
quiz.explanation: A frequently-changing hierarchy makes Visitor's core trade-off work against you instead of for you.

quiz.question: What's a textbook real-world use of Visitor?
options: Walking a compiler's abstract syntax tree with different visitors for type-checking, code generation, and formatting
Managing undo/redo history in a text editor
quiz.answer: Walking a compiler's abstract syntax tree with different visitors for type-checking, code generation, and formatting
quiz.explanation: AST traversal is the classic case: a stable set of node types, with many operations performed on them over time.
